video.title: How a classifier decides
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — your computer studies teacher, Kenya (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: A busy morning market. Mr Joseph stands at a fruit stall piled with mangoes, green to yellow. The seller presses one gently with her thumb, glances at its colour, and hands it over with a smile. Joseph turns the mango in his hand, curious.
scenes.animation: A small press ring pulses where the thumb presses (150 ms); a colour swatch slides from green to yellow under the mango. Quick push-in on Joseph’s face.
scenes.narration: At the market this morning, a mango seller judged a mango in two seconds. One squeeze, one look at its colour: “Eat it tomorrow.” She’s handled thousands, so she compares. Can a computer do that?

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and a yellow ‘AI’ track chip with the spark icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how a classifier decides, by asking its neighbours.

scenes.visual: A single mango in the middle. Two slider gauges grow beside it: ‘softness’ from 0 to 10, and ‘colour’ from a green 0 to a yellow 10. Each slider’s marker slides to the mango’s value: 7 and 8. A ruler icon stamps the word ‘features’ beneath.
scenes.animation: Gauges draw in left to right (300 ms); markers slide to their values (600 ms).
scenes.narration: A computer can’t squeeze a mango, so we describe it with numbers. Softness, from zero to ten. Colour, from green at zero to yellow at ten. Measurable numbers like these are called features.

scenes.visual: A chart draws itself: softness along the bottom, colour up the side. Checked mangoes drop onto it as dots: filled circles (ripe) settle in the top-right corner, open squares (not ripe) in the bottom-left.
scenes.animation: Axes draw (400 ms); dots drop in quickly with a tiny bounce, ripe ones first, then the others.
scenes.narration: Now put every mango you’ve checked on a chart: softness along the bottom, colour up the side. Each is a dot, marked ripe or not. Ripe ones gather in one corner, unripe in the other.

scenes.visual: A new mango appears on the chart as a triangle, between the two corners. Three leader lines reach out to its three closest dots: two filled circles and one open square. A tally shows 2 against 1, and the triangle turns into a filled circle.
scenes.animation: Leader lines draw one by one (200 ms each); the tally counts up; the triangle morphs into a circle.
scenes.narration: A new mango arrives, with no label. Find the three closest dots: its nearest neighbours. Two are ripe and one isn’t, so the majority says ripe. No rules, just: which mangoes is it most like?

scenes.visual: Clean white card with the AI track chip. The word ‘classifier’ appears above two labelled boxes, ‘ripe’ and ‘not ripe’. A new example slides in and drops into one box. Below, a small stack of stored examples and a raised-hands ‘vote’ icon.
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in (200 ms); the example drops in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: A classifier is a model that puts a new example into a class, like ripe or not ripe. Nearest neighbours is one simple kind: it compares the new example with stored ones, and goes with the majority.

scenes.visual: A grandmother in a courtyard looks up at heavy grey clouds. Thought bubbles show three remembered days with the same clouds; two of them end in rain. She takes the washing off the line, smiling to herself.
scenes.animation: Thought bubbles pop in one by one (200 ms); rain drops fall in two of them; the washing slides off the line.
scenes.narration: It’s like a grandmother who can tell when it will rain. She remembers days that felt like today: the same heavy air, the same dark clouds. Most of them ended in rain, so she takes the washing in. Her nearest neighbours are the days most like today!

scenes.visual: Ms Salma pops in beside the chart: a new mango with five leader lines, to three filled circles and two open squares. Three answer cards drop in below her.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A new mango’s five nearest neighbours: three ripe, two not. What does the classifier say?

scenes.visual: The card ‘Ripe: three of five’ gets a blue check badge. Then a dial labelled k turns: at 1, the new mango’s single neighbour is an odd, mislabelled dot; at 15, the circle of neighbours stretches across the chart and grabs faraway dots; at 5, it settles.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms). The neighbour circle grows and shrinks with the dial (600 ms each).
scenes.narration: Ripe: three of its five neighbours are ripe. But the number you ask, called k, matters. Ask only one, and a single odd or mislabelled mango decides. Ask too many, and faraway mangoes outvote close ones. In between usually works best.

scenes.visual: Split screen. Left: the softness and colour chart, ripe and unripe dots neatly apart. Right: a chart of weight alone, where big ripe and big unripe mangoes sit side by side in one jumbled line, and a new mango’s neighbours disagree.
scenes.animation: Both charts draw at once; on the right, the dots shuffle into a jumble (600 ms).
scenes.narration: Features matter as much as neighbours. Softness and colour separate ripe from unripe, so close neighbours agree. Weight alone doesn’t: a big unripe mango sits right beside a big ripe one, and its neighbours mislead.

scenes.visual: A phone screen showing the ‘Nearest neighbours’ lab: mangoes on a chart of softness and colour, filled circles and open squares, a shaded background showing the answer everywhere, a slider for k and a switch for ‘With mistakes’. A finger taps the chart; leader lines reach to the neighbours.
scenes.animation: The tap ripples (150 ms); leader lines draw; the slider moves and the shaded background shifts.
scenes.narration: In the app, mangoes sit on a chart: filled circles are ready to eat, open squares not yet. Tap to place a new mango, then slide k from one to fifteen and watch the answer change. Then try the data with mistakes.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds up a page of handwritten digits: sevens and ones in different hands and inks. Three answer cards appear beside him.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Your model must tell handwritten sevens from ones. Which feature helps more?

scenes.visual: The ‘How wide the digit is’ card gets the check badge, then the screen resolves into four summary lines and a closing line.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in one by one, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: How wide the digit is: a seven is wider than a one, whatever the ink. Remember: describe each example with features you can measure. A new example takes the class of most of its k nearest neighbours. And choose features that separate classes.

scenes.visual: A student at a kitchen table with ten tomatoes and a sheet of squared paper, scoring each one and marking dots on a hand-drawn chart. A new tomato gets three pencil lines to its nearest dots. Mr Joseph gives a thumbs up. End card: the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Dots appear one by one on the paper; the three pencil lines draw. End card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: score ten fruits for size and softness, from zero to ten. Mark each on a chart, labelled ripe or not. Then score a new fruit, and let its three nearest neighbours decide.

checkpoints.prompt: A new mango’s five nearest neighbours: three ripe, two not ripe. What does the classifier say?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — most of its neighbours are ripe, so it says ripe.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — it needs no rules. It goes with the majority: three of its five neighbours are ripe.

checkpoints.prompt: Your model must tell handwritten sevens from ones. Which feature helps more?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a seven is wider than a one, whoever writes it and in any ink.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — ink colour and names don’t change the digit. Width does: a seven is wider than a one.
